scenes.visual: osprey dives toward a school of menhaden over plankton, then a three-link chain with question marks
scenes.tts: Ospreys nest along the Chesapeake Bay. They plunge feet-first into the water to catch fish. In parts of the Bay, one fish they often bring home is the Atlantic menhaden. Menhaden are small fish that eat plankton, tiny living things that drift in the water. So here is the question. Why does each step up this food web have less energy to live on?

scenes.visual: sun sends energy to phytoplankton (producer); zooplankton eat them (first-order consumer)
scenes.tts: Nearly every food web starts with a producer. A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in food. In the open Bay, the main producers are phytoplankton, tiny drifting algae. Many zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, eat phytoplankton. They are first-order consumers.
scenes.narration: Nearly every food web starts with a producer. A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in food. In the open Bay, the main producers are phytoplankton, tiny drifting algae. Many zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, eat phytoplankton. They are first-order consumers.

scenes.visual: food chain of five chips, arrows from food to eater, consumer orders labelled
scenes.tts: A food chain is a straight-line model of one path that energy takes. The arrows point from the food to the eater. In this chain, menhaden eat zooplankton, so here they are second-order consumers. Menhaden also eat phytoplankton directly. Ospreys eat menhaden. A third-order consumer eats second-order consumers. So the osprey is a third-order consumer here.

scenes.visual: bar of energy in the plankton a menhaden eats splits into heat, undigested, and body
scenes.tts: A menhaden eats plankton. Most of that energy does not become new menhaden. Much of it is given off as thermal energy, which is heat. Some of the food passes through the fish without being digested. Only the rest is built into the fish's body, where an osprey can get it.

scenes.visual: four-block energy pyramid with made-up numbers, one tenth per step, heat arrows
scenes.tts: Stack the energy of each level as a block. This stack is an energy pyramid. As a rough rule, about one tenth of the energy in one level is available to the next. Here is a model with made-up numbers. Producers have ten thousand units. First-order consumers have one thousand. Second-order consumers have one hundred. Third-order consumers have ten.

scenes.visual: pyramid with sunlight in and heat out at every step; answer text
scenes.tts: So here is the answer. At each step, much of the energy is given off as heat. Energy does not disappear. It changes form. Only roughly one tenth is left for the next level. In most ecosystems, energy flows one way, in as sunlight and out as heat. And an energy pyramid is not a head count.
